query: Starting from a W–Cu composite containing W particles or interconnected W ligaments within a Cu matrix, what single intervention could overcome phase separation and interfacial void formation, thereby improving thermal conductivity relative to the untreated composite under heat-transfer and irradiation conditions relevant to joints between W-based plasma-facing materials and Cu-based cooling components? Formulate one hypothesis that states the intervention, the proposed mechanism, the predicted comparative outcome, the applicable processing and service boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Integrating a thin, reactive Ni‐rich interlayer on the tungsten surfaces prior to composite consolidation will modify the interfacial chemistry so as to suppress phase separation and void formation during service-like heat-transfer and irradiation conditions, thereby enhancing the effective thermal conductivity of the W–Cu composite.
generation.material_initial_state: A W–Cu composite comprised of either discrete tungsten particles or an interconnected network of tungsten ligaments embedded in a copper matrix that, when exposed to high heat flux and irradiation, exhibits phase separation at the W/Cu interfaces and formation of interfacial voids.
generation.intervention: Introduce a thin Ni‐rich coating on the tungsten surfaces (via deposition or pre-alloying) before composite processing so that the resultant interface becomes reactive and forms a stable Ni‐enhanced intermetallic phase with both W and Cu.
generation.conditions: The processing (pre-coating and subsequent composite consolidation) and service conditions—namely, high heat-transfer rates and irradiation environments typical of joints between W-based plasma‐facing components and Cu-based cooling systems.
generation.structural_mediator: A modified interfacial region in which the Ni interlayer promotes enhanced atomic interdiffusion between W and Cu, leading to the formation of a coherent, finely dispersed Ni‐rich intermetallic or solid solution phase that reduces interfacial energy and void nucleation sites.
generation.mechanism: The Ni interlayer improves wettability and bonding between tungsten and copper. This promotes a stable, chemically graded interface that relieves local strain and suppresses thermodynamic driving forces for phase separation and void formation. In turn, this stabilized interface maintains continuous thermal conduction paths despite cyclic thermal loading and irradiation-induced defects.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to untreated W–Cu composites, the Ni-coated composites will exhibit a lower density of interfacial voids and reduced phase separation, resulting in an improved effective thermal conductivity under conditions of heat transfer and irradiation representative of plasma-facing joint applications.
generation.baseline: The untreated W–Cu composites typically experience phase separation and interfacial void formation under operative thermal/irradiation conditions, which degrades their thermal conductivity.
generation.boundary: This improvement is expected to be effective within the temperature (roughly 500–1000 °C) and irradiation regimes relevant to plasma-facing and cooling component joints. The intervention’s effectiveness may be limited if the Ni-induced interfacial phase is unstable under extreme irradiation or prolonged thermal cycling beyond these conditions.
generation.uncertainty: While interfacial modification by reactive coatings is known to enhance bonding in metal composites, the precise kinetics of interfacial phase formation and stability under simultaneous irradiation and high heat flux remain to be fully quantified.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two groups of identically processed W–Cu composites. For the experimental group, apply a thin Ni‐rich interlayer onto the tungsten phase (using physical vapor deposition or an equivalent method) prior to composite consolidation. Subject both the Ni-coated and the control (untreated) samples to cyclic heating and controlled irradiation that mimic operational conditions in plasma-facing joints. Post-treatment, perform detailed microstructural analysis and thermal conductivity measurements.
measurements: High-resolution SEM/TEM imaging to quantify interfacial void density and phase homogeneity at the W–Cu interfaces
XRD or APT analysis to detect the formation and stability of the Ni‐rich interfacial phase
Laser flash analysis or equivalent thermal diffusivity measurements to determine thermal conductivity variations pre- and post-treatment
Irradiation damage assessment via TEM after exposing samples to a known dose
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Ni-coated composites do not exhibit a statistically significant reduction in interfacial void formation or phase separation, or if their measured thermal conductivity under simulated heat-transfer/irradiation conditions does not improve relative to the control samples, then the hypothesis is falsified.
